options: Word order is not what she is learning here.
The sounds are unchanged; the meaning is new.
She is long past babbling.
Right: semantics is about what words and sentences mean.

why.correct: Cooing (about 2 months), babbling (about 6 months), one word (about 12 months), telegraphic speech (about 18 to 24 months).
Harlow’s results challenged the idea that infants bond because they are fed.
options: Right: soft touch, not food, drew the infants to the cloth mother.
Neither artificial mother moved; the infants chose comfort.
The infants left the wire mother as soon as they had fed, so food was not what bonded them.
Egocentrism is about taking another’s point of view.

why.correct: Secure attachment lets a child explore because comfort is available when needed.
options: Separation anxiety is distress when the caregiver leaves, not comfort when present.
Parenting styles describe how parents set rules and show warmth, not a cloth figure.
Parallel play is children playing side by side.
Right: a securely attached child uses the caregiver as a base, returning for comfort and then venturing out.

why.correct: Animal research must minimize pain and distress; these studies produced lasting harm.
options: Debriefing applies to human participants after deception.
Sample size is a design concern, not why the studies are judged unethical.
Right: protection from harm, including for animals, weighs heavily against causing lasting distress.
Animals never give informed consent; committees judge harm and benefit instead.

why.correct: Generalizing from animals to people needs supporting human evidence, which attachment research later provided.
options: Harlow controlled which mother had milk; the problem is generalizing across species.
Right: results from rhesus monkeys must be checked in human research before generalizing.
Monkeys share much with humans, but species differ.
The monkeys still went to the wire mother to feed.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>30</mn><mn>50</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{30}{50} \times 100 = 60\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
The reunion is the key moment for classifying attachment.
options: A secure baby may be upset when the parent leaves and seeks comfort at reunion, then calms.
An anxious baby is very upset at separation and both clings and resists at reunion.
A disorganized baby shows confused or contradictory behavior, such as freezing or approaching while looking away.
Right: little distress at separation and turning away at reunion mark avoidant attachment.

why.correct: Anxious babies want comfort but cannot easily be soothed by it.
options: An avoidant baby shows little distress and ignores the parent at reunion.
Distress at separation shows an attachment exists; the reunion shows what kind.
Right: intense distress and a mix of clinging and resisting at reunion mark anxious (ambivalent) attachment.
A secure baby is comforted by the parent’s return and goes back to playing.

why.correct: Generalizing depends on how similar the participants are to the population named.
options: Attachment is clear by about 8 to 12 months.
Right: participant characteristics such as culture and income limit generalization; avoidant and anxious rates differ by country.
Generalization is judged from who the participants are, not mainly from sample size.
It was developed for human infants.

why.correct: Outer layers affect a child indirectly through the people in the inner layers.
options: Right: a setting the child is not in that still affects him through others is the exosystem.
The microsystem holds settings Luis is directly part of, like home and school.
The mesosystem is the links between two of Luis’s own settings, such as home and school.
The macrosystem is the broad culture, values and laws.

why.correct: The mesosystem is about how a child’s settings connect.
options: Home and school each are microsystems; the link between them is the mesosystem.
The exosystem holds settings the child is not part of.
The chronosystem is change over time.
Right: connections between two of the child’s settings, home and school, form the mesosystem.

why.correct: Culture, laws and the economy shape the settings that shape the child.
options: The law does not link two settings the baby is in.
Ecological systems theory says outer layers do affect children, through inner ones.
Right: laws and cultural values are in the outermost layer and work through the inner ones.
The law is a broad social policy, not a direct setting.

why.correct: The chronosystem adds time to the other layers.
options: The exosystem is a setting the child is not in, at one time.
Right: changes over time, including historical events, form the chronosystem.
The microsystem is a child’s direct settings at a given time.
The mesosystem is the links between settings.

why.correct: Authoritative parenting combines high demands with high responsiveness.
options: Right: high warmth plus clear, explained limits is authoritative parenting.
Authoritarian parents set strict rules with little warmth and expect them to be followed without discussion.
Permissive parents are warm but set few rules or limits.
Disorganized is an attachment classification, not a parenting style.

why.correct: The names are close: authoritarian is the strict, cold style; authoritative is the warm, firm one.
options: Authoritative parents explain their rules and are warm.
Permissive parents set few rules.
Avoidant is an attachment classification of a child, not a parenting style.
Right: strict rules, no explanations and little warmth.

why.correct: Correlation is not causation, and influence runs both ways between parents and children.
options: A relationship was found.
Children can influence parents, but this reverses the finding.
Right: these are correlational findings; easygoing children may draw out warm, reasoned parenting, and effects differ across cultures.
The studies are correlational, and the pattern varies across cultures.

why.correct: Temperament is present early, is partly heritable, and shapes how others respond to a child.
options: Attachment forms over the first year through caregiving.
Right: from birth, babies differ in mood, activity and how they react to change.
Nothing suggests different parenting; the differences appeared at birth.
Identity statuses describe adolescents and adults exploring who they are.

why.correct: Separation anxiety shows the baby has a special bond and understands the caregiver is gone.
options: Right: distress at separation from a caregiver typically appears around 8 months and peaks in the second year.
An avoidant baby shows little distress at separation.
Egocentrism is difficulty taking another’s point of view.
This is about the baby’s reaction, not how the parent raises him.

why.correct: Play becomes more social and more imaginative across the preschool years.
options: This reverses the order.
The second scene involves make-believe roles.
In the first scene they are not pretending or playing together.
Right: playing side by side comes first; shared make-believe comes later.

why.correct: Identity statuses combine two questions: has the person explored, and have they committed?
options: Moratorium is exploring without yet committing.
Diffusion is neither exploring nor committing.
Right: she explored options and then committed.
Foreclosure is committing without exploring, often by adopting parents’ plans.

why.correct: Commitment without exploration is foreclosure.
options: He has a firm commitment.
Right: he committed without exploring other options.
Achievement requires exploring before committing.
He has committed, so he is not still exploring.

why.correct: The imaginary audience and personal fable describe a kind of teenage egocentrism.
options: Right: teens often feel that others are watching and judging them far more than they are.
The personal fable is believing one is unique or invulnerable, not that others are watching.
This is about commitment to a path without exploring.
The social clock is about when life events are expected to happen.

why.correct: The personal fable includes feeling unique, and sometimes invulnerable.
options: That is the feeling of being watched and judged.
That is a status of having explored and committed.
That describes an infant’s distress when a caregiver leaves.
Right: believing one’s experiences are unique, so no one else could understand them.

why.correct: Each of Erikson’s stages pairs a task with the risk of not meeting it.
options: That young-adult stage is about forming close relationships.
That adolescent stage is about building a sense of self.
Right: in late adulthood, people look back and feel their life was meaningful (integrity) or full of regret (despair).
That middle-adult stage is about contributing to the next generation through work and caring.

why.correct: Generativity means caring for and guiding the next generation.
options: That is infancy’s stage of learning whether needs will be met.
Right: middle adults find purpose by contributing to the next generation.
That is late adulthood’s look back on life.
That is the school-age stage of building competence.

why.correct: Around ages 1 to 3, the task is doing things for oneself.
options: Right: toddlers build independence; support helps, harsh criticism breeds doubt.
That earlier stage is about whether an infant’s needs are reliably met.
That preschool stage is about planning and starting activities.
That school-age stage is about mastering skills.

why.correct: Emerging adulthood is linked to longer schooling and later marriage, so it is more common in some cultures than others.
options: That is a teen’s sense of being watched.
She is exploring, not committing without exploring.
That is an infant’s distress when a caregiver leaves.
Right: in many wealthy countries, the years from about 18 to the mid-20s are a time of exploring before settling down.

why.correct: The social clock varies across cultures and generations.
options: That is an inborn style of reacting.
That is the links between a child’s settings.
Right: a culture’s expected timing for events like marriage and parenthood.
That is feeling unique or invulnerable.

why.correct: Felitti and colleagues (1998) found a dose-response pattern: more ACEs, higher average risk. ACE scores are a screening tool, not a prediction for one person.
options: ACEs include neglect and household problems too.
Right: the link is strong across groups, and many people with high scores do well, especially with supportive relationships.
The finding is a population-level association; many people with ACEs stay healthy.
The study found a clear link.

why.correct: Possible selves motivate action toward a hoped-for self and away from a feared one.
options: Right: images of who we might become, hoped-for and feared, can guide what we do now.
Her thoughts are about her future, not about being watched.
She is exploring a direction, not drifting without one.
This is about her own thinking, not a parenting style.

why.correct: A single taste paired with illness, even with hours between them, is enough: the sushi became a CS that now triggers nausea (the CR).
options: Right: one pairing of a taste with illness, even hours apart, made the sushi a conditioned stimulus for nausea.
Habituation is a weaker response to a repeated stimulus. Jordan reacts more, not less.
Spontaneous recovery needs an earlier extinction. Nothing was extinguished here.
Higher-order conditioning pairs a new stimulus with an existing CS. The sushi was paired directly with illness, the UCS.

why.correct: Her fear spread from one kind of large dog to similar dogs: stimulus generalization.
options: Right: stimuli similar to the original CS (other large dogs) now trigger the CR.
Discrimination is responding to the CS but not to similar stimuli. Maya responds to the similar ones.
Extinction weakens a CR. Her fear has spread, not faded.
Habituation would make her react less to dogs over time, the opposite of what happened.

why.correct: The can opener has been paired with food and the blender has not, so the cat responds to one and not the other: discrimination.
options: Right: the cat responds to the stimulus paired with food and not to a similar one that never was.
Generalization would mean running to the blender too.
Spontaneous recovery is a CR returning after extinction and a rest; nothing was extinguished.
Food is the UCS and needs no learning. The cat has learned which sound predicts it.

why.correct: Habituation is the simplest learning: a response fades to a stimulus that repeats without consequence. It needs no pairing, which is what sets it apart from extinction.
options: Right: a repeated stimulus that brings nothing important produces a weaker and weaker response. No pairing is involved.
Extinction weakens a learned CR when a CS stops being paired with its UCS. Waking to a loud noise was never conditioned.
Discrimination is telling a CS apart from similar stimuli, not reacting less to one stimulus.
Counterconditioning pairs a stimulus with a new, opposite response. Nothing was paired here.

why.correct: The smell was paired with the song, a stimulus that was already conditioned, not with the partner directly: higher-order (second-order) conditioning.
options: Right: the song was already a CS, and pairing the smell with that CS made the smell a CS too, with no UCS present.
Generalization is a response to stimuli similar to the CS. A smell is not similar to a song.
Taste aversion pairs a taste with illness and produces nausea, not happiness.
Spontaneous recovery is an extinguished CR returning after rest. Nothing was extinguished.

why.correct: Counterconditioning pairs the CS (the chair) with a UCS that triggers a response incompatible with fear, so calm replaces fear.
options: Right: the feared CS is paired with stimuli that bring a pleasant, incompatible response, which replaces the fear.
Spontaneous recovery is a CR coming back after extinction, the opposite of what the dentist wants.
Higher-order conditioning pairs a new stimulus with an existing CS to spread a response, not to replace it.
Generalization spreads a response to similar stimuli. Here the response to one stimulus changes.

why.correct: Preparedness: natural selection favored ancestors who learned quickly to fear real dangers, so those links form faster and resist extinction.
options: Right: evolution has primed people to learn some links, such as fear of snakes, more easily than others.
Habituation is a weaker response to repeated stimuli. It does not explain why one kind of picture is learned faster.
People did discriminate the two kinds of pictures, but that does not explain why snakes were learned faster.
Spontaneous recovery is a CR returning after extinction. This is a difference in how fast a CR is acquired.

why.correct: Extinction weakens a CR but does not erase the learning. After a rest, the CR can come back for a while: spontaneous recovery.
options: Right: an extinguished CR returns, usually weaker, after a rest period.
Acquisition is the first learning of the link. Nothing new was paired with the car.
Habituation would make his response weaker over time, not bring it back.
Generalization is a response to stimuli similar to the CS. The car is the CS itself.

why.correct: Only the link from the CS to the CR is learned. The UCS to UCR link is inborn.
options: Right: the CR is a learned response to a stimulus that once did nothing.
The UCR is automatic: no learning is needed for food to cause salivation.
The UCS triggers its response with no learning; that is what "unconditioned" means.
Salivating to food is an inborn reflex, the UCR. It is not learned.

why.correct: Behaviorism holds that psychology should study observable behavior and how the environment shapes it.
options: Right: behaviorism studies observable behavior and the events that predict it.
Inner thoughts cannot be observed directly, so a strict behaviorist sets them aside.
Diaries report inner experience. Behaviorism focuses on what can be observed and measured.
Hidden wishes are not observable behavior, which is what behaviorism studies.

why.correct: Today an IRB would require that participants, especially children, are protected from lasting harm. The study is also a single case, so how well it generalizes is unclear.
options: Right: the researchers created a lasting fear in an infant and did not undo it.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard, and this was a single case.
The main problem was not shared data but harm done to the child.
Blinding protects against bias in results. It is not the safeguard this study failed.

why.correct: A neutral stimulus, a UCS that already works, repeated pairing, the CS alone producing the CR, then the CR spreading to similar stimuli.
A UCS triggers a response with no learning: the puff of air makes the eye blink (the UCR).
options: Right: the puff causes a blink without any learning.
Before training the tone is the neutral stimulus; it caused blinks on only 5% of trials.
That is the conditioned response, a learned blink.
The sensor measures blinks. It is part of the method, not a stimulus.

why.correct: After acquisition, the tone (CS) alone triggers a blink (CR). The same movement is a UCR when the puff causes it and a CR when the tone does.
options: Right: the tone is now a CS and the learned blink to it is the CR.
The UCR is the blink to the puff. No puff was given on these trials.
A neutral stimulus causes no relevant response, and a blink to it after training is learned.
A blink is a response, not a stimulus.

why.correct: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished CR after a pause. It went from 10% at the end of extinction to 45% the next day.
options: Right: after extinction and a rest, the CR came back, weaker than before.
That rise is acquisition: the tone becoming a CS.
That fall is extinction, the tone presented without the puff.
That is the baseline, before any learning.

why.correct: An operational definition says exactly how this study measured the variable: blinks detected by the sensor within half a second of the tone, as a percent of tone-alone trials.
From trial 9 the tone came alone, so the CR (saliva to the tone) faded: extinction.
options: Right: when the CS is no longer followed by the UCS, the CR weakens.
Food was not given on these trials, so the dog could not habituate to it.
There is one tone in this study, so there was nothing to discriminate.
Trials 9 to 15 happened on the same day; the rest came after trial 15.

why.correct: A CR that returns after rest (spontaneous recovery) means extinction suppressed the response rather than wiping out what was learned.
options: Right: spontaneous recovery shows the CS to CR link survived extinction.
No new stimulus was paired; a UCS is not acquired anyway.
A tone never causes saliva without learning, so it cannot be a UCS.
The same tone was used, so this is not generalization.

why.correct: Add the five values, <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 26</annotation></semantics></math>, and divide by 5: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>26</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{26}{5} = 5.2</annotation></semantics></math> drops.
Spontaneous recovery on the next day shows the learned link was still there, only suppressed.
options: Right: if the link were gone, the tone alone would bring no saliva after rest.
That rise shows acquisition. It says nothing about whether extinction erased the link.
That plateau shows learning leveled off before extinction began.
Zero drops at trial 15 is what the student points to; it does not argue against the claim.

why.correct: "Negative" means something is removed and "reinforcement" means the behavior increases. The beeping is removed, and buckling up increases.
options: Right: buckling up removes an unpleasant stimulus (the beeping), so buckling up increases.
Punishment makes a behavior less likely. Buckling up became more likely.
Negative punishment removes something wanted and lowers a behavior. Ravi lost nothing he wanted.
Positive reinforcement adds something wanted. Here something unpleasant was taken away.

why.correct: Think of the behavior that changes: coming home late. It decreases (punishment), because a wanted thing was removed (negative).
options: Right: something wanted (the phone) is removed, and the behavior (coming home late) decreases.
Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant and increases a behavior. Losing the phone is not removing something unpleasant.
Positive punishment adds something unpleasant, such as extra chores. Here something was taken away.
Extinction is no longer reinforcing a behavior. The parents added a consequence instead.

why.correct: Name the behavior first (being late). It decreases, so this is punishment; something unpleasant was added, so it is positive.
options: Right: an unpleasant consequence is added, and lateness decreases.
Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant and increases a behavior. Laps were added, and lateness fell.
Negative punishment removes something wanted. Laps are added, not taken away.
A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need and increases a behavior. Laps lower the behavior.

why.correct: Shaping reinforces closer and closer approximations of a behavior the animal would rarely produce on its own.
options: Right: reinforcing successive approximations, each closer to the target behavior.
Instinctive drift is an animal sliding back toward inborn behavior. The trainer is building a new behavior.
Higher-order conditioning pairs a stimulus with a CS. The trainer is rewarding behaviors the dog makes.
Superstitious behavior comes from accidental reinforcement. These rewards are planned.

why.correct: Reinforcement strengthens whatever came just before it, even when there is no real link. That accidental link is superstitious behavior.
options: Right: a behavior that happened to come just before a reward was reinforced by accident.
Shaping is planned reinforcement of steps toward a goal. Nobody planned this.
Learned helplessness is giving up after events seem uncontrollable. She is acting, not giving up.
Discrimination is responding to one stimulus and not similar ones. It is not about her own behavior being rewarded.

why.correct: Instinctive drift: learned behaviors can slide back toward behaviors the species does by instinct, which limits what conditioning can teach.
options: Right: the animal drifts back toward an inborn food-getting behavior (rooting) that competes with the trained one.
Superstitious behavior is reinforced by accident. Rooting was never reinforced; it delayed the food.
Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished conditioned response, not a slide toward an inborn behavior.
Shaping builds a target behavior step by step. The rooting moved away from the target.

why.correct: Learned helplessness: after experiences that seem uncontrollable, a person or animal stops trying to escape or succeed, even when control is possible again.
options: Right: after repeated outcomes she could not control, she stops trying even when trying would now help.
Negative reinforcement would increase a behavior by removing something unpleasant. Her studying stopped.
Instinctive drift is a slide toward inborn behavior, such as a pig rooting.
Shaping builds a behavior step by step through reinforcement. Nothing is being built here.

why.correct: Money, grades, points and stamps are secondary (conditioned) reinforcers: they work because they lead to primary ones.
options: Right: they gained value by being linked to something already rewarding.
Primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs, such as food or warmth. A stamp does not.
A negative reinforcer is something unpleasant that is removed. Stamps are added.
That is a classical conditioning term for a stimulus that triggers a reflex. Stamps trigger no reflex.

why.correct: Classical conditioning links two stimuli and changes reflex-like responses; operant conditioning links a behavior to its consequence and changes how often the behavior happens.
options: Right: a voluntary behavior changes because of its consequence.
This is a reaction to a signal paired with pain: classical conditioning.
Watering at a signal for food is a classically conditioned response.
The flinch is a reaction to a stimulus paired with a startling bang: classical conditioning.

why.correct: Posts appear after unpredictable stretches of time, not after a number of checks: a variable-interval schedule, which produces slow, steady checking.
options: Right: new posts arrive after unpredictable amounts of time, and the first check after one arrives is rewarded.
A fixed-ratio schedule rewards every set number of responses, such as every fifth check. Posts do not arrive that way.
A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time, such as a post every hour on the hour.
Continuous reinforcement rewards every response. Often there is nothing new.

why.correct: Pay per 20 boxes is a fixed ratio. More responding brings more pay, so the rate is high, with a pause after each reinforcer.
options: Right: a fixed-ratio schedule produces high response rates with a brief pause after each reinforcer.
That scalloped pattern belongs to a fixed-interval schedule, paid by time.
That pattern fits a variable-interval schedule.
A ratio schedule keeps paying for responses, so work continues.

why.correct: Scallops (slow, then fast, then a pause at each set time) are the signature of a fixed-interval schedule.
options: Right: responding is slow after a reinforcer and speeds up as the set time approaches, giving a scalloped curve.
A variable-ratio schedule gives the fastest, steadiest curve, with no pauses. That is curve A.
A fixed-ratio schedule gives fast responding with brief flat pauses after each reinforcer. That is curve B.
A variable-interval schedule gives slow, steady responding with no scallops. That is curve C.

why.correct: On a variable ratio every press could be the one that pays, so there is no reason to pause: the fastest, steadiest curve.
options: Right: reward after an unpredictable number of presses keeps responding fast and steady.
Short pauses after each reward are typical of a fixed ratio.
Slow steady responding fits a variable interval: more presses do not bring rewards sooner.
Scallops fit a fixed interval.

why.correct: Curve C reaches 450 presses at 30 minutes: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>450</mn><mn>30</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{450}{30} = 15</annotation></semantics></math> presses per minute.
Ratio schedules reward the number of responses, so responding faster earns more. Interval schedules reward the first response after time passes, so faster responding earns little.
options: Right: ratio schedules pay for responses, interval schedules pay for the passage of time.
Nothing in the data shows hunger, and the difference matches the known effect of schedule type.
Continuous reinforcement rewards every press. Curve C is described as unpredictable.
Extinction lowers responding over time; curve A rises steadily.

why.correct: A manipulated variable (the schedule) plus random assignment makes it an experiment.
options: Right: they manipulated the reward schedule and randomly assigned students to the two groups.
A correlational study measures variables as they occur. Here the schedule was manipulated.
Students were placed in a controlled game the researchers designed, not watched in daily life.
A case study looks closely at one person or a few. This compared two groups of 20.

why.correct: Partial (intermittent) reinforcement produces behavior that lasts longer in extinction than continuous reinforcement does.
options: Right: when rewards were already unpredictable, a run of no rewards does not signal that rewards have ended.
The every-time group, on continuous reinforcement, quit sooner. Continuous reinforcement gives fast learning but fast extinction.
No unpleasant stimulus was removed when students pressed.
Learned helplessness follows uncontrollable events. The every-time group had full control until points stopped.

why.correct: In order: 58, 64, 71, 82, 90. The middle value is 71 presses.
Persistence was the count of presses after points stopped, which is how this study measured it.
Vicarious reinforcement: seeing a model rewarded makes the observer more likely to imitate.
options: Right: Mia saw a model rewarded and became more likely to copy the behavior herself.
Mia was never rewarded herself, so her behavior was not directly reinforced.
Latent learning is learning that stays hidden until a reason to show it appears. Mia learned from watching a model be rewarded.
Generalization is a conditioned response spreading to similar stimuli. Mia copied a behavior.

why.correct: The employee learned from a model's consequence, not their own: vicarious punishment.
options: Right: seeing a model punished makes the observer less likely to do the same.
Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant after the person's own behavior and increases it.
Learned helplessness is giving up after uncontrollable events, not avoiding a behavior a model was punished for.
Insight learning is a sudden solution to a problem.

why.correct: Insight: the solution appears suddenly, after a pause, as a whole, the way Wolfgang Köhler described his chimpanzees doing.
options: Right: a sudden grasp of how the parts of a problem fit together, not gradual trial and error.
Shaping needs a trainer to reinforce steps. The chimp solved it alone, all at once.
Latent learning is earlier learning that shows up when a reward appears. This is a new solution reached suddenly.
Superstitious behavior is strengthened by accidental reinforcement; this is purposeful problem solving.

why.correct: He formed a mental map of the city (a cognitive map) without reinforcement, and it showed once he had a reason to use it: latent learning.
options: Right: he learned the layout without a reward, and it showed when he needed it.
No one reinforced steps toward walking the route.
He did not watch anyone being rewarded for walking that route.
Habituation is a fading response to a repeated stimulus, not knowledge of a layout.

why.correct: Modeling: observing and imitating a model's behavior. Note that this link is correlational in real data, so other factors (shared homes, friends, access) also play a part.
options: Right: people imitate the behavior of models, especially models they identify with.
Instinctive drift is a trained animal sliding toward inborn behavior.
Taste aversion is a learned avoidance of a food after illness.
Habituation is a weaker response to a repeated stimulus, not copying someone.

why.correct: Vicarious punishment lowers performance, not learning. With an incentive, the learned behavior appears.
options: Right: learning and performance differ. The behavior was learned through observation and appeared once it paid.
They copied it immediately when asked, so it was already learned from the video.
Learned helplessness is giving up after uncontrollable events. The children acted as soon as there was a reward.
Watching changed both what they learned and, before stickers, what they did.

why.correct: Insight is sudden, whole and often comes after a pause; gradual improvement through repeated attempts is trial and error.
options: Right: the violinist improves gradually; the friend reaches a sudden, whole solution.
The violinist's gradual improvement is not insight, which is sudden.
Neither person is copying a model, and the violinist's progress is visible, not hidden.
No model is copied by the friend; no trainer shapes either one.

why.correct: Attention to a model, and the motivation to copy it, rise when the model is similar, warm, high in status or rewarded.
options: Right: models seen as similar, admired or successful are imitated more.
The finding says the opposite: some models are imitated more than others.
Observational learning changes behavior without direct reinforcement.
Children imitate a great deal without instruction, and the finding is about who the model is.

why.correct: Reward circuits that use dopamine respond most to rewards that are better than expected, one neurological factor in learning.
options: Right: dopamine signals in reward circuits track surprising rewards, which helps strengthen the behavior that came before.
The finding shows brain activity linked to learning.
Reward signals matter in operant learning too; the scenario is about a treat after a behavior.
Food is a primary reinforcer. The question is about the brain signal.

why.correct: Bandura described attention, retention (memory), reproduction and motivation. Without attention and memory, nothing can be copied.
options: Right: attention and memory (retention) come before reproduction.
Observational learning can happen with no reward to the observer.
Punishing the model lowers imitation; it is not a required step.
Shaping is operant training, not part of learning by observation.

why.correct: Their sudden drop means the learning happened earlier, unrewarded, and was revealed once a reward appeared: latent learning.
options: Right: latent learning. Food gave them a reason to use a cognitive map they already had.
Learning the maze from scratch took the always-fed rats about ten days, so one day is too fast.
The never-fed rats improved a little, and the day-9 group shows unfed rats learned the layout.
Habituation would mean a weaker response to the maze, not fewer wrong turns once food appeared.

why.correct: Exploring without food, the rats built a mental representation of the maze, a cognitive map.
options: Right: a mental picture of the maze's layout.
Taste aversion is a learned dislike of a food after illness.
